llms-how-they-work.context_blurb: A large language model, usually shortened to LLM, is the kind of program that sits underneath chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. You type in plain English and it writes back. Underneath, it is not thinking the way a person thinks, and it is not looking anything up on the live web. It is a very large statistical pattern-completer, trained once on huge piles of text and then put to work predicting what piece of text is likely to come next, over and over. Everything you see a chatbot do — write an essay, explain a topic, roleplay a character, work through a math problem — is that same mechanism dressed up with a chat wrapper. Knowing this is the single most important piece of AI literacy. It explains almost every strength (fluent writing on well-known topics, quick summaries, patient re-explanation) and almost every weakness (confidently wrong on specifics, bad at multi-step arithmetic, drifting across long conversations, no idea what happened yesterday). It also explains why a chatbot can sound exactly as confident when it is wrong as when it is right: fluency and accuracy are separate properties, and the training rewards fluency. Hold on to this picture — pattern-completer, not thinker, not database — and almost every chatbot story in the news starts to make sense.

transformers-and-attention.context_blurb: Modern AI chatbots are built on a particular design of neural network that overtook the field in the late 2010s. Every major chatbot you have heard of uses it underneath. The design's defining trick is that it lets the model consider many words of the conversation at the same time, in parallel, instead of reading one word after another the way older AI language systems worked. That change made it practical to train on huge datasets using the kind of hardware ordinarily built for video-game graphics, which is why the current AI boom is so tied to specialized chip supplies. This family of architectures is the quiet engine behind almost everything in the current AI era — chatbots, coding tools, image models, multimodal systems. Media coverage from this decade onward will keep assuming you know what this family is called, so recognizing the name on sight is worth more than any one technical detail about how it works. Several researchers at a large US tech company introduced the design in a single academic paper, which the field now treats as foundational — a surprising amount of modern AI history traces back to a handful of such papers, and this one is near the top.

tokens-and-context-window.context_blurb: When you talk to a chatbot the model does not actually read whole words the way you do. It chops your text into small pieces and processes those. That chopping scheme is why models sometimes spell words strangely or miscount letters — the model is not working at the letter level. The second idea that goes with those pieces is a fixed limit on how much of the current conversation the model can still see at once. Modern chatbots have large but finite limits here. When a chat gets long enough, the oldest parts fall out of the window and the model loses track of them — names you established, decisions you made, facts you set up. The two concepts together explain a lot of odd chatbot behavior: why models sometimes spell strangely, why very long chats start to drift or forget what you said, why pasted documents have size limits, and why models tend to pay less attention to information buried in the middle of a very long prompt. In practice, a chatbot's 'memory' in a long conversation is a budget rather than a filing cabinet — once the budget overflows, the earliest content is gone unless the chat product has been designed to save notes between sessions, which is a separate feature bolted on top.

neural-networks-and-deep-learning.context_blurb: A neural network is the engine under almost every modern AI system. The name comes from a loose mid-twentieth-century analogy to brain cells, but the thing itself is pure math: layers of simple arithmetic units stacked between the input and the output, with huge numbers of adjustable settings inside that get tuned during training. The 'deep' in deep learning just means many layers. For most of AI's history this family of techniques was unpopular; it took off only once computers and datasets got large enough for it to work. The three researchers most associated with keeping the approach alive during the lean decades were later awarded the field's top computing prize together — one of the clearest cases in modern science of long-unfashionable research paying off. This is the common machinery behind image recognition, chatbots, voice assistants, and self-driving perception — one family of methods applied across many places that used to look like unrelated problems. Recognizing the family name and the fact that it is not literal 'brain modelling' (it is math inspired by a very loose analogy) is useful literacy, because popular writing often slides from the metaphor into claims the technology does not actually make.

training-pretraining-inference.context_blurb: An AI chatbot gets built in two very different stages. The first is long, slow, enormously expensive: the model studies piles of text and adjusts its many internal numbers. This happens once (or a few times) per model, often costing enormous amounts of money, running on huge clusters of specialized chips, consuming lots of electricity. The second stage is much cheaper and faster: using the trained model to answer each question, one chat reply at a time. The split matters because almost every important AI business and policy question — chip supply, data use, model releases, running AI on your own computer, export controls, environmental impact — ties back to the distinction between the one-time stage and the many-times stage. The useful thing to notice is that once a model has been through the first stage, the resulting file of trained numbers can in principle be copied, shipped, or run anywhere compatible hardware exists; the company that made it can control access only if it keeps the file to itself. That single property divides the AI industry into its two big camps — labs that ship only through controlled interfaces and labs that release the trained file publicly.

fine-tuning-and-rlhf.context_blurb: A raw trained language model will happily continue any text, including unhelpful or offensive output. To turn it into something that behaves like a polite assistant, labs add a second stage of training on top. One version of this takes the pre-trained model and gives it extra practice on a narrower task or style — think of it as specializing the generalist. Another version uses human raters to compare pairs of answers and nudges the model toward answers that rate higher. This was the breakthrough step that turned raw next-word predictors into useful chatbots. This stage matters because it is where the model picks up its personality, its refusal patterns, its polish — and, unavoidably, the values of whichever people were doing the rating. Measured studies have found systematic political and cultural leanings in major chatbots that trace back to this stage: which raters were hired, what instructions they were given, which responses were rewarded. 'Alignment' is the industry word for this shaping work, but alignment is never a neutral default. It is editorial, and recognizing that is a useful literacy skill for making sense of model-behavior stories in the news.

hallucination.context_blurb: A core failure mode of modern chatbots is producing confident, fluent, completely false content. The word the industry has settled on for this is a loaded one, but it names a real pattern: the model generates plausible-sounding text that turns out to have no basis in reality. It is not a bug the next version will patch away — it is a structural feature of how these systems work. The model is predicting plausible next words; it has no internal fact-checker and no connection to a database of truth. The failure clusters on specifics — exact dates, exact names, numbers, citations, URLs — because those are the places where many plausible-looking strings fit the pattern and only one is actually right. Broad descriptions ('this physicist made important contributions') tend to be fine; narrow specifics ('she won the Nobel in 1927 for a paper published in Nature') are where the failure shows up. The confident tone of the wrong answer is the dangerous part — the model produces invented court cases, fake citations, and made-up biographical facts in exactly the same style as real ones. Learning to recognize this pattern, and to treat chatbot specifics as hypotheses to verify rather than facts to repeat, is central to using any AI tool safely.

embeddings-and-vector-search.context_blurb: An embedding is the trick that lets AI treat meaning as a kind of geometry. Each word, sentence, or document gets turned into a long list of numbers — a point in a high-dimensional space. Points that mean similar things end up near each other; points that mean different things end up far apart. This is why modern AI can find a document about 'fixing a leaky faucet' when you asked about 'repairing a dripping tap' — the words are different but the meaning-points are close. The idea quietly powers search, recommendations, memory features in chatbots, and the retrieval step in retrieval-augmented systems. One famous early demonstration showed that these spaces capture semantic structure: certain meaningful concepts turn out to live as consistent directions in the number-space, so arithmetic on the embeddings can shift meaning predictably. This is one of modern AI's foundational tools — not because the technical details matter, but because the pattern 'turn meaning into numbers so it can be searched geometrically' underlies a huge amount of what modern consumer AI products do when they say 'understanding your query' or 'personalizing your results.'

scaling-laws-and-model-size.context_blurb: A striking finding of the modern AI era is that bigger tends to work better in a predictable way. If you make the model's parameter count larger, use more training data, and run more compute, the resulting model gets reliably better at predicting text — the gain follows a smooth mathematical curve rather than jumping around. Labs use these predictions to decide, before spending huge sums on a training run, roughly what a bigger model is likely to do. The scaling story is why frontier training runs now cost many hundreds of millions of dollars, why chip orders can swing national trade balances, and why the AI industry is remaking the geography of data centers and electricity. At some scale, qualitative new abilities emerged that smaller models did not show — the ability to pick up a new task from a few examples in the prompt, for one. This is contested territory: there are signs the easiest gains from pure scale may be slowing as the simplest 'make it bigger' approach runs into limits of available high-quality data and electricity. Nobody is certain how far it goes, and the scaling-vs-architecture argument is one of the field's live debates.

mixture-of-experts.context_blurb: Mixture of Experts, usually shortened to MoE, is a design that lets a model have a huge total parameter count while using only a small slice of those parameters on any given question. The internal network is split into many parallel sub-networks, and a small router inside the model decides which of them to activate for each incoming piece of text. The practical result is that total model capacity (which affects what the model knows) can grow much faster than the compute cost of answering any one question. The practical point: when a lab reports that a model has, say, hundreds of billions of parameters total but only a few dozen billion active per token, this is probably why. The architecture is how recent frontier models get bigger in capacity without getting proportionally slower or more expensive to run. It also matters for openness debates — a large MoE model is bigger to download than a dense model with the same per-token compute, which makes 'running it locally' harder in practice even when the weights are freely available.

multimodal-ai.context_blurb: A multimodal AI model is one that handles more than one kind of input in the same system — text plus images, sometimes also audio and video. Earlier chatbots only read text. A modern multimodal chatbot can take a photo you upload and discuss it, listen to a voice note, or watch a short video. The trick underneath is that every kind of input gets converted into the same sort of numerical representation and fed through the same core network — images get sliced into small patches that are treated almost like text tokens, audio gets turned into similar numerical pieces, and the model learns to work across all of them at once. This is why the current flagship chatbots can describe pictures, transcribe speech, help with code snippets, and discuss documents interchangeably. Recognizing the label will matter more and more as AI products get built around voice, cameras, and video rather than only typed text. It also matters for safety: once a model can read images, instructions hidden in images (image prompt injection) become a possible attack path that pure-text models did not have.

open-weight-vs-closed-api.context_blurb: Modern AI models come in two shapes that look similar from the outside but are structurally very different. Some only run on their company's servers; you talk to them through a controlled interface, and your conversation goes to the company. Others release the trained numbers as a downloadable file, so anyone with the right hardware can run them locally, modify them, or build on them. This distinction drives a long list of policy fights — about safety, privacy, competition, export controls, chip export rules, and who ends up in charge of frontier AI. The debate splits along real tradeoffs: closed models let a lab control misuse by filtering requests and refusing certain actions, while open models prevent a small group of companies from being the only ones who can run the technology. Once a capable model is released openly, it cannot be recalled — the file exists on thousands of hard drives and shows up on peer-to-peer networks. Safety training applied to the weights can be removed with modest fine-tuning. These are structural trade-offs, not rhetorical ones, and recognizing them is more useful than picking a side.

chatgpt-and-openai.context_blurb: OpenAI is the San Francisco lab that made ChatGPT. It started as a research outfit with an ambitious public mission about safe artificial intelligence, then restructured its finances later so it could raise the money needed to train frontier models — a shift its critics have argued broke the founding promise. ChatGPT launched as a research preview and quickly became one of the fastest-growing consumer products on record, moving this new kind of content-creating AI from research demo to household tool in a matter of weeks. The company has been at the center of nearly every major AI story since — product launches, lawsuits over training data, governance crises, personnel changes, and the industry push for federal regulation. Its complicated relationship with a very large investor from the broader tech industry has shaped much of what the company can and cannot do; much of what looks like OpenAI activity is in practice happening on that investor's data centers. If you only learn to recognize one AI company, this is the one. Recognizing the names of its CEO, its co-founders who later left, and its signature chatbot product on sight is a floor-level AI literacy skill.

claude-and-anthropic.context_blurb: Anthropic is a US AI lab, led by siblings serving as CEO and President, that builds one of the best-known chatbots. Its founding team left another well-known AI lab citing disagreements over the pace of frontier development and the balance between research and product. Anthropic positions itself as unusually focused on AI safety research, and the name of its chatbot was chosen as a nod to a famous twentieth-century mathematician whose foundational work on information theory sits somewhere behind all modern computing. One of its signature training techniques uses an explicit written list of principles given to the model, letting the model critique and revise its own outputs against those principles rather than relying only on crowd-rated examples. The lab is one of the handful of frontier labs you will encounter again and again in AI news. It is also a case study in a specific corporate form (a Delaware public-benefit corporation) that allows directors to weigh public benefit against shareholder return — though enforcement of that weighting is mostly internal rather than external, so recognizing the structure without over-trusting it is the right posture.

gemini-and-google-deepmind.context_blurb: Google is one of the oldest serious players in AI. Its two internal AI groups were merged into a single organization, called Google DeepMind, led by DeepMind's co-founder. The merged lab builds the model family and chatbot product called Gemini. Google has an unusual mix of history: its researchers helped invent the architecture underneath every modern chatbot, its DeepMind arm produced the breakthroughs on games and protein folding that are the defining non-chatbot accomplishments of modern AI, and yet Google was slow to ship a consumer chatbot. OpenAI reached the public first, which shocked the industry. Gemini is Google's major catch-up push, and you will meet it in search results, Android phones, and the Google Workspace apps. Google's integration with search and advertising gives Gemini a different distribution footprint than its competitors — the model does not need to persuade users to visit a new product; it shows up where users already are. That reach cuts both ways: when a tuning choice goes wrong, as happened with the Gemini image generator, the reach makes the resulting mess much more visible.

xai-and-grok.context_blurb: Elon Musk was one of OpenAI's early funders before leaving its board in the late 2010s. After ChatGPT's success he publicly complained about OpenAI's direction, filed lawsuits over its shift away from the original non-profit mission, and launched a new AI lab of his own. Its chatbot is deeply integrated with the social-media platform Musk also owns, giving it real-time access to the platform's posts and a different content-moderation posture from the mainstream US chatbots. The chatbot's name is borrowed from a mid-twentieth-century science-fiction novel. Recognizing this history matters because the Musk-OpenAI feud shapes a huge share of public AI commentary. The new chatbot is explicitly sold as a counterweight to mainstream chatbots, with lighter refusal patterns and a 'maximally truth-seeking' pitch; whether the resulting tuning is more neutral or just differently tuned is itself a contested question, and recognizing that the question exists is more useful than taking either side's word for it.

llama-and-meta-open-weight.context_blurb: Meta — the company formerly called Facebook — is one of the frontier AI firms, and its approach is distinctive. While most other leading US labs ship closed-API chatbots that only run on their own servers, Meta releases its flagship models as downloadable files that anyone can run locally. The family has become the backbone of the open-source AI ecosystem; the first release leaked onto peer-to-peer networks within days, after which Meta leaned into deliberate openness with subsequent versions. The usual read on this strategy is competitive rather than selfless: when you cannot be the leader of a closed platform, commoditizing the layer below weakens the leaders. Meta's role in open-weight AI is the main reason capable local models exist at all. Recognizing this piece of the industry matters because much of the practical AI privacy story — running models on your own hardware, keeping prompts off company servers — depends on Meta's open releases plus the ecosystem of smaller open-weight labs that have followed. The openness policy also complicates the simple story that AI is concentrated in a few closed labs.

deepseek-and-chinese-ai.context_blurb: A Chinese AI lab broke into Western attention in late 2024 and early 2025. Its openly-released models matched the capability of leading US frontier models while reportedly costing a small fraction of US training budgets. The release shook two assumptions at once: that frontier AI required US-scale spending, and that chip-export controls could keep capable models out of China. The lab was founded and funded by a Chinese hedge-fund manager, which is itself an unusual profile for a frontier AI effort. This lab is the headline example that frontier AI is no longer a US monopoly, and that algorithmic efficiency can rival pure scale. The policy implications ran in several directions at once: open-weight advocates saw a vindication of their approach; US-first strategists saw a case for tighter export controls; critics of regulatory-capture arguments noted that national-security framings make it easier for incumbents to argue for restrictions. Chinese data-sharing law adds another layer — Chinese companies are legally obligated to cooperate with state intelligence requests, which complicates the simple 'open-weight is private' story in the Chinese case.

mistral-and-european-ai.context_blurb: A French AI lab, founded by former researchers from two large labs, ships open-weight language models that anyone can download and run. The lab has become the main European entry in a field otherwise dominated by US and Chinese firms, and it has been publicly critical of parts of EU AI regulation on the grounds that heavy rules favor large incumbents over open-source challengers. Recognizing this lab matters because Europe's AI story is often told as a regulatory one — the EU's AI legislation, GDPR, product-liability directives — and this lab is the main counter-example of a European lab actually competing on capability. The policy argument matters more broadly: compliance costs that a large US lab can absorb from a dedicated compliance team can be crushing for a smaller company, so even well-intentioned regulation can entrench exactly the firms it was supposed to constrain. Both sides have real arguments here, and recognizing the tension between regulation and openness is part of understanding the debate.

microsoft-ai-partnerships.context_blurb: Microsoft is not a frontier AI lab in the same way as the smaller specialized firms, but it is one of the single most important actors in the AI industry — because of how it partners with those labs. Microsoft's enormous investment in one of the leading US AI labs made that lab's compute possible and gave Microsoft deep product integration: a chat-powered search product, assistants in Office, features in Windows. The partnership was tested during a late-2023 governance crisis at the lab, when Microsoft was ready to absorb the lab's whole team within hours — an offer that in practice forced the governance crisis to resolve in favour of continuity. Recognizing Microsoft's role matters because much of what looks like independent AI-lab activity is in practice happening on Microsoft's data centers and distribution channels. The dependency is structural, not just financial — the lab's training cannot easily move to a different cloud provider mid-run, which gives Microsoft leverage even where the formal legal relationship might suggest otherwise. Regulators have taken notice: the US Federal Trade Commission opened an inquiry into whether the partnership effectively functions as a merger.

image-generators.context_blurb: These are the AI tools that take a written description — 'a knight reading a book by candlelight' — and produce a matching picture. The three names worth knowing are the one from a well-known US AI lab (named after a surrealist painter and a Pixar robot), an independent lab that originally ran its service through a chat platform popular with gamers, and a model released with open weights that triggered an explosion of fan-built derivatives. Underneath, they share a general approach that learns to turn noise into images step by step by training to reverse that noising process on real images. The quality improvements between versions come from better-curated training data and more compute, but the underlying method stays the same. These tools are where many people first meet generative AI and where many of the practical recognition challenges — fake images, hands with wrong finger counts, letter-shaped gibberish in images, uncanny background details — live. The open-vs-closed split from the broader AI industry shows up here too: open image models are harder to restrict and easier to misuse, which is the usual tradeoff.

voice-assistants-and-speech-ai.context_blurb: Voice assistants on phones and smart speakers have been part of consumer life for well over a decade. They work in two stages: a small model on the device listens for a trigger phrase, then the audio after it is sent to the cloud, turned into text by speech-recognition AI, and processed. Open-source speech-to-text models now transcribe dozens of languages at high quality, which is transforming journalism, accessibility software, and medical transcription. The main providers each have their own: a trigger phrase for a well-known phone-maker's assistant launched with an iPhone, a different one for a major online retailer's smart speaker, a third for Google's assistant, a fourth for Microsoft's older voice product. This family of tools is worth knowing because the always-listening microphone pattern — trigger phrase, cloud processing, logged audio, occasional misfires that send audio to the cloud that was never meant to leave the room — is a core piece of modern consumer AI and a core privacy consideration. The pattern is also where modern voice-cloning scams meet consumer-recorded voice data: that recording of you saying 'hey, it's me' is useful training material for someone impersonating you later.

alan-turing.context_blurb: The man at the center of this topic was a British mathematician — probably the single most important figure in the pre-history of computer science and AI. He spent his short career on two kinds of problem: the mathematical foundations of what any computing machine can do, and whether a machine could ever be said to think. He also worked on highly classified wartime code-breaking for the British government, work that remained secret for decades after the war ended and may have shortened World War II substantially. His writing from the mid-twentieth century still frames the way philosophers and engineers argue about AI capability today — in particular, a thought experiment he proposed for whether a machine could be said to think, based on a conversational game between a human and a machine with a hidden judge trying to tell them apart. He published his AI thinking in a philosophy journal, an unusual choice for a working mathematician that reads today as a deliberate reach into the humanities. He is one of the handful of thinkers whose work directly set up the modern era of AI, and a tragic biographical figure in his own right.

john-mccarthy.context_blurb: The man at the center of this topic was an American computer scientist who gave this whole field its name. In the mid-1950s he organized a famous summer research workshop that put the phrase into the world. The workshop itself produced no big technical results, but it launched AI as an organized research field with a name and a community, which the pre-existing cybernetics tradition had not provided. McCarthy went on to design one of the earliest high-level programming languages, a language built around lists and symbolic expressions that became the dominant tool of classical AI research for decades, and he later founded a famous AI lab at a West Coast research university after leaving MIT. His collaborator from the summer workshop founded a parallel lab on the East Coast, and the two labs anchored US AI research for a generation. He put the field's now-famous name into circulation and, with a small number of mid-century collaborators, defined the field as a thing that could be funded, taught, and argued about.

eliza-and-early-chatbots.context_blurb: Before the modern AI era, researchers built a surprising number of what we would now call chatbots. One famous example from the 1960s pretended to be a therapist by pattern-matching whatever the user typed and reflecting it back as a question. Another, from around the same period, could carry on simple conversations about a tabletop world of colored blocks, demonstrating what looked like real language understanding inside a tightly constrained setting. Both programs impressed people — their own authors told stories about colleagues forming attachments to them — and both exposed a lasting pattern: humans will project mind and understanding onto almost any program that produces plausible conversation. The therapist program's author went on to become a thoughtful critic of the field, arguing that some decisions — judging, listening, caring — should stay with humans even when machines can simulate them. The blocks-world program's limits also exposed a recurring AI pattern: performance inside a constrained simulation often did not transfer to the messy real world. Both lessons are among the oldest and most durable in AI.

ai-winters.context_blurb: An AI winter is a period when funding and interest in AI collapse because the field has over-promised and under-delivered. The first big one followed a critical government-commissioned report on AI research in the UK in the 1970s, which concluded that AI's grand promises were not panning out at the research scale that worked for easy problems. UK AI funding was cut for a decade afterward. A second winter arrived in the late 1980s when a different AI approach that had actually been deployed in businesses failed to live up to its hype — this hit industrial budgets rather than only academic ones, which made the retreat sharper. A high-profile Japanese national project built around a specific logic-based approach was wound down as part of the same disappointment. The pattern worth recognizing — confident timeline, big promises, disappointment, funding collapse — has repeated across AI's history and informs skepticism about today's timelines. The content of the predictions is different each cycle, but the shape is familiar enough that anyone who recognizes it can keep a cool head when the next 'AGI by 2027' headline lands.

deep-blue.context_blurb: IBM built a chess computer that defeated the reigning world chess champion in a six-game match in the late 1990s. This was the first time a reigning world champion had lost a match to a machine, and it was one of the AI milestones a generation grew up waiting for. The important recognition point: the chess computer worked by classical computer-science techniques — brute-force search of millions of positions per second plus hand-crafted chess rules — not by any deep-learning method. It was 'good old-fashioned AI' at its peak, and this is often forgotten in retellings that make it sound like a modern neural-network achievement. The champion later accused the IBM team of receiving human help during games, which IBM denied; the controversy reflected the surprise of a dominant human player meeting a machine that could play positionally in a way no previous engine had. After the match, each new AI milestone (Go, poker, protein folding, chatbots) has been measured against this moment. Recognizing the chess-computing era as its own kind of AI — distinct from the modern neural-network era — is a useful piece of historical literacy.

ibm-watson-jeopardy.context_blurb: In the early 2010s IBM Research built a natural-language question-answering system named for the company's founder and entered it in a famous US TV quiz show. It beat two of the show's greatest living champions on live television. The match showed that an AI system could handle punny clues, retrieve relevant facts, and wager strategically. The losing champion's final written answer became a viral quip. IBM then tried hard to turn the technology into a business — especially in healthcare and consulting — and that part largely did not work out. The healthcare rollout became an industry cautionary tale: a confident benchmark-winning system that could not match the operational and clinical demands of real hospitals. The arc is worth recognizing because the pattern recurs: a flashy benchmark win does not automatically translate into useful real-world products. Modern AI has its own version of this problem, with the leaderboard-topping model that cannot ship a reliable customer-facing product sitting alongside the quietly-useful tool nobody wrote headlines about.

imagenet-and-alexnet.context_blurb: In the mid-2000s a Princeton computer-vision researcher assembled a huge collection of labelled images — millions of pictures sorted into thousands of categories by crowd-workers hired through an online marketplace — and it became the standard benchmark for the field. In the early 2010s a graduate team at a Canadian university entered a competition built on that dataset and won by such a large margin that it is widely considered the start of the modern deep-learning era. Within a year, image-recognition labs around the world switched to the same family of techniques. The winning entry was named after one of the graduate students on the team. One of the enabling pieces of hardware was graphics processors originally built for video games, which turned out to be perfect for training large neural networks because they could do many simple math operations in parallel. This episode was the match-strike that lit the current AI boom. The dataset, the model, and the researchers all deserve recognition as the foundations of what came after — most of modern AI traces back to that specific pair of years.

geoffrey-hinton.context_blurb: Geoffrey Hinton is a British-Canadian computer scientist, long associated with a Canadian university, often called a godfather of modern AI. He helped make a crucial neural-network training technique famous in a mid-1980s paper, led the team that won the foundational early-2010s image-recognition contest together with two of his graduate students, and later shared the field's top computing prize for the body of work. He spent about a decade at one of the big US tech companies before resigning so he could speak publicly about AI risk. He subsequently shared a Nobel Prize for his foundational work on learning in neural networks. In public he tends to focus on concrete near-term harms — disinformation at scale, autonomous weapons, large-scale labor disruption — rather than the more apocalyptic framings that some other voices in the field use. Recognizing him as a specific voice with a specific position matters because news coverage often flattens him into a generic 'AI pioneer worried about AI' quote, which blurs the real content of what he actually argues.

yann-lecun.context_blurb: Yann LeCun is a French-American computer scientist, one of the chief AI figures at a major US tech company (the one formerly called Facebook), and one of the three researchers awarded the field's top computing prize together for deep-learning work. He is best known technically for an image-focused family of neural networks he developed in the late twentieth century at Bell Labs — an approach that eventually enabled modern image recognition and medical imaging applications. In public debates he is the most prominent frontier researcher pushing back against AI-doom framings. He argues that current language models lack the goal-directed agency, self-preservation drives, and recursive self-improvement that catastrophic scenarios assume, and that the real worries are more ordinary (misuse, bias, concentration of power). Recognizing his position is useful because most AI-risk reporting assumes a one-sided debate he is not part of — treating the 'frontier researchers all worry about extinction' line as obvious when in fact one of the top researchers in the field spends a substantial portion of his public time disagreeing.

yoshua-bengio.context_blurb: Yoshua Bengio is a French-Canadian computer scientist, long associated with one French-speaking Canadian city, and the third member of the trio who shared the field's top computing prize for deep-learning work. He founded a leading academic AI research institute in Quebec, now one of the world's major non-corporate deep-learning centers. On AI risk his posture sits between those of his two co-laureates: he has supported safety governance, signed open letters urging caution, and co-authored papers on AI safety, while continuing active technical research. It is a reminder that the field's leaders disagree openly — and that there is no single 'what the researchers think' to quote on AI's trajectory. News coverage that treats one of these three as a stand-in for 'all AI researchers' is misreading the field's structure. The three share credit for the foundations of modern AI and part company on what to do next, which is useful literacy for interpreting any 'AI researcher says X' headline.

demis-hassabis-deepmind.context_blurb: Demis Hassabis is the British co-founder of a famous London AI research lab, now part of Google. He was a chess prodigy as a child, reaching master-level rating as a teenager, then designed successful video games in his teens and twenties before earning a doctorate in cognitive neuroscience and turning to AI research full-time. He founded his lab in London with two co-founders, and Google acquired it a few years later for a large sum. Under his leadership the lab produced the breakthroughs on Go, chess, and protein folding that are the defining non-chatbot accomplishments of the modern AI era. He later shared a Nobel Prize for the protein-folding work. He is one of the clearest counter-examples to the stereotype that modern AI only produces chatbots — the non-chatbot track of applied AI, especially in biology and game-playing, runs through his lab. Recognizing him as a specific figure with a specific research trajectory matters because the 'frontier AI' coverage is often dominated by chatbot companies in a way that leaves out the parts of the industry doing substantive scientific work.

turing-award-deep-learning.context_blurb: The field's top computing prize — often called the Nobel Prize of computing — went jointly in the late 2010s to three researchers who had championed neural networks for decades, mostly while the field considered the approach a dead end and favored other methods. Their shared award, arriving after the 2012 image-recognition breakthrough and shortly before the ChatGPT moment, is a case study in long-unfashionable research paying off: for about twenty years, going into neural networks was going into a career dead end, and the three of them continued the work anyway. All three remain active public voices in AI, often disagreeing with each other about where the field is going and what the real risks are. Recognizing this trio as the architects of the deep-learning era makes it easier to place the researchers whose names show up most often in AI news. It is also a useful counter to the implicit framing that AI is a technology without specific authors — these are specific people who made specific choices, and their choices shape what the industry looks like today.

alphago-lee-sedol.context_blurb: AlphaGo was a Go-playing AI program built by Google's London research lab. In the mid-2010s, in a televised multi-game match played in South Korea, it defeated one of the top human Go players of his generation. The match was the most-watched AI event before ChatGPT, especially in East Asia where Go is a serious cultural institution — a game that has been played at a professional level for more than a thousand years. Go had been considered a hard target for AI because its board is much larger than a chessboard and the search space is vastly bigger; computer scientists had predicted that top-human-level play was decades away. The match is widely cited as the cultural and investment turning point for the modern AI era — afterwards, the money and attention flooded in, and the field entered the funding and talent cycle that led directly to the chatbot boom a few years later. The human champion later retired from professional play, citing AI's dominance as a central reason. This is the pre-chatbot AI breakthrough that still matters.

alphazero-self-play.context_blurb: AlphaZero was a later DeepMind system that generalized the AlphaGo recipe. Where the Go-focused system had been trained in part on recorded human games, this successor started from only the rules of the game and taught itself to play by playing against itself over and over. The same single algorithm reached superhuman play across multiple games with clean rules, including chess and a Japanese chess variant. A later version of the system even learned the rules themselves from play. The result mattered because it showed that in a domain with clear rules and a clear winner, deep reinforcement learning could rival or surpass centuries of accumulated human expertise — no human examples required. The headline-maker in chess was the system's win rate against the then-strongest classical chess engine, achieved with vastly less raw search per move but much better evaluation. Recognizing the self-play method matters because it defines what AI is good at (games with closed rule sets and clear outcomes) and what it is still bad at (open-ended, context-dependent human problems where rules and outcomes are themselves contested).

alphafold-protein-folding.context_blurb: AlphaFold is a DeepMind system that predicts the 3D shape a protein folds into from its chain of amino acids. The problem had been one of biology's famously hard open questions for about half a century — a classical puzzle about how a long chemical chain settles into one specific shape among astronomically many possibilities. Experimentally working out a single structure often took a graduate student years of careful laboratory work. The system's breakthrough result at an international competition and the open database that followed transformed structural biology; the database contains predictions for essentially every protein known to biology, freely available to any researcher. The DeepMind team behind it later shared a Nobel Prize for the work, jointly with a US researcher who had been developing a related approach to designing brand-new protein molecules from scratch. This is the clearest example of modern AI doing something a traditional lab cannot — and the clearest case where releasing scientific results broadly, rather than locking them up as proprietary, has multiplied the real-world impact of the work.

ai-in-medicine.context_blurb: AI tools have been quietly used in medicine for longer than most people realize. Modern image-classification systems can spot lung nodules, breast lesions, diabetic eye changes, and certain skin cancers at performance comparable to skilled specialists. The typical deployment is not 'replace the doctor' but 'second reader' — the human reads the scan first, then the AI checks for anything the human might have missed, with the human staying in charge of the final call. One autonomous AI system has received regulatory clearance for diagnosing diabetic eye complications directly, letting primary-care offices screen patients who would otherwise never see a specialist in time. AI is also used to narrow the search for candidate drug molecules, speeding up early-stage discovery. Clinical trials in humans still take years because safety and efficacy testing is irreducibly slow. The pattern across medical AI is the same: real speedups in narrow parts of the pipeline, with humans still doing the judgment work, within workflow and liability frameworks that benchmark papers do not capture.

ai-in-agriculture-weather.context_blurb: Beyond chatbots and image generators, AI is quietly in use in a lot of everyday infrastructure. In farming, modern systems use real-time computer vision to tell weeds from crop rows and spray herbicide only where it is needed, cutting chemical use substantially and reducing runoff into nearby water. Satellite imagery combined with crop-specific neural networks lets farmers see field-scale stress — drought, pests, nutrient deficiency — before it is visible from the ground, in time to adjust irrigation or harvest timing instead of discovering the problem at harvest. In weather forecasting, trained networks can produce forecasts far faster than the traditional physics-based supercomputer models, learning atmospheric patterns from decades of historical data instead of simulating the physics step by step. Faster forecasts have real consequences: minutes saved on a hurricane track can mean lives saved through earlier evacuation. The main limitation is that models trained on past patterns can underestimate rare extreme events outside their training data — exactly the cases where accuracy matters most.

self-driving-cars.context_blurb: Self-driving has been one of the longest-running AI promises. The state of play in the mid-2020s is a split. One well-known US operator runs truly driverless robotaxis in several cities using a heavy sensor stack of laser scanners, radar, and cameras — but only inside pre-mapped, geofenced zones where the vehicle's behavior has been tested. Another well-known car maker ships driver-assistance software on general roads, with cameras only, and the human driver remains legally and practically responsible. The naming of the second company's software has drawn repeated criticism, because the name oversells what the system actually does and some drivers have treated the assistance as full autonomy with fatal consequences. A third US operator lost its operating permit in a major city after a serious pedestrian incident and a disclosure failure to regulators. The pattern to notice: narrow-but-real driverless capability inside mapped zones, versus a much harder 'anywhere a human can drive' problem that is not solved.

code-assistants.context_blurb: AI code assistants read what a programmer is writing and suggest the next lines. The first widely-used example came out of a partnership between a major software platform and an AI lab in the early 2020s and quickly reached millions of professional developers. More recent tools are built around a language model with access to the whole project — the user can type a feature request and the tool drafts changes across multiple files. These tools genuinely speed up boilerplate work, routine tests, and translation between languages, but they can also suggest insecure patterns, deprecated libraries, or subtly wrong logic. Code-assistant output in a programmer's name is still the programmer's responsibility to read, test, and understand. Studies through the mid-2020s reported real time savings on well-scoped tasks but no clear shrinkage of overall software-engineering employment — the pattern was 'less typing boilerplate, more reading AI output, more system design, more debugging AI mistakes.' Recognizing the shift matters because it is a preview of how AI changes a profession rather than ending one.

machine-translation.context_blurb: Automatic translation is one of the oldest AI applications and one of the ones that has improved the most dramatically. For a long time, services used statistical word-frequency models and hand-written grammar rules that produced famously stilted output. In the mid-2010s the leading services switched to a new kind of learned model trained on huge amounts of parallel text — sentences already translated by humans into both languages — and quality jumped. The main limitation today is that translation quality still tracks the amount of parallel training data, so major language pairs do much better than low-resource ones; low-resource languages are exactly the ones where improvement would matter most for the people speaking them. For high-stakes work (legal contracts, literary translation, technical specifications) AI translation is a draft, not a final — fluent but confident-wrong output is a specific failure mode where the errors can be subtle enough to pass review. Recognizing when a translation needs a human reviewer is a useful AI-literacy skill.

recommendation-systems.context_blurb: This is the kind of AI underneath 'what you might watch next.' Different platforms optimize for different measurable goals; some are notorious for how fast they learn what holds a given user's attention from tiny signals like watch time and rewatches. These systems are not optimizing for whether the content is true, balanced, or good for you. They optimize for whatever measurable number was chosen as the goal — usually some count of how much people watch and interact — and multiple studies have found that doing so pulls viewers toward more intense and emotional content, because that is what holds attention longest. A core technique behind many of these systems is collaborative filtering: find users whose history overlaps with yours, recommend what they liked that you have not seen yet. This is a core modern-media pattern, not an accident. Every recommendation is a bet based on your past behavior and others like you about what will hold your attention next — the algorithm does not know what will be good for you, and the metric it does know is picked to grow the platform.

ai-in-science.context_blurb: The AI-in-science story goes well beyond protein folding. In chemistry, neural networks trained on huge databases of known compounds are proposing novel candidate materials and new antibiotic molecules; one well-publicized case identified a new antibiotic by scanning millions of molecules for predicted antibacterial activity. In mathematics, systems have surfaced statistical patterns in mathematical data that let human mathematicians spot and then prove new theorems — the AI as research collaborator rather than as prover. Large tech labs have reported millions of candidate crystal structures found this way, though the honest counts of 'genuinely novel useful materials' are much smaller than the headline numbers. The honest summary across these cases: real acceleration of early discovery and screening, with experimental validation still slow, and headline 'discovery' counts needing careful follow-up before they can be taken at face value. Recognizing this category — AI as scientific co-worker — matters because it is where some of the technology's most durable value may end up sitting, even if the chatbot side gets most of the press.

spotting-ai-text.context_blurb: AI-generated text has subtle but recognizable fingerprints. The writing tends to be polished, balanced, and hedged — because the training rewarded that style — and tends to overuse certain phrases that happen to appear often in the kinds of writing the models were trained on. Specific punctuation marks and formatting choices get used far more often than a typical human writer uses them. Sentence structures become repetitive. Paragraphs tend to balance pros and cons even when the actual answer is clear. Transitional phrases pile up. These tells are useful at a glance but they are not proof — many humans write that way, especially non-native English speakers writing formally, and AI tools are learning to vary their style. AI-text detectors have real false-positive rates that have caused real harm to students who did not cheat. Recognizing the pattern is a literacy skill, not a verdict: it tells you to look harder, not to accuse someone. The broader concern worth recognizing is stylistic convergence — if a huge share of public writing starts routing through similar AI tools, the full range of human voice narrows in ways that are hard to see one text at a time.

spotting-ai-images.context_blurb: AI image generators produce impressive pictures most of the time and then slip in characteristic ways on fine details. Certain body parts are famously harder than the rest of the picture for the model to get right — hands with wrong finger counts or impossible joints, ears rendered asymmetrically, teeth with strange arrangements. Small objects that touch skin or hair are often rendered wrong: earrings melting into skin, glasses fusing with faces, hair blending oddly into jewelry. Text inside the image comes out as letter-shaped marks that read convincingly at a glance but spell nothing — the model learned what letters look like without a built-in model of how spelling works. Reflections in glass and shadows from off-screen light sources often fall the wrong way, because the model has no 3D scene underneath. The underlying reason for all of these is that these models learn visual patterns of what things look like without a built-in model of what things are. Spotting these flaws is a learnable habit that gets harder as the tools improve, which is why the general practice of 'verify unusual images through other sources' matters more than any one tell.

deepfake-video-audio.context_blurb: A deepfake is a video or audio clip that AI has altered to make a real person appear to say or do something they did not. The tech grew out of face-swap research in the mid-2010s and matured quickly once consumer tools shipped. Video tells tend to appear at the boundary between the real footage and the swapped parts: mouth movements drift slightly out of sync with speech, especially on lip-closing consonants; fuzzy edges around hair or jewelry; blinking patterns that are off in older models. The attack scaled to real corporate finance once multi-person video deepfakes became possible — a well-publicized Hong Kong case authorized a very large transfer on a video call where every face except the victim's was synthetic. For individuals, the key defense is out-of-band verification: when something is important, confirm through a different channel before acting. A deeper problem is the 'liar's dividend' — once any video could be a deepfake, real video evidence can also be dismissed as fake. The recognition skill is not to trust individual tells but to build the habit of verifying unexpected clips through established sources before reacting.

voice-clone-scams.context_blurb: AI voice-cloning tools can produce a convincing imitation of a specific person from only a short clip of audio — a voicemail, a social-media video, a podcast appearance. 'Grandparent scams' using cloned voices extend an old scam pattern: a 'relative' calls in distress and asks for emergency money, pressing urgency so the victim is rushed past their better judgment. The scale shifted when consumer services brought the audio requirement down from minutes to seconds and the cost down from professional-studio to free-tier. The simplest fast defense is a short phrase only your family members know, agreed in advance in calm conditions before any scammer applies pressure — a scammer with a voice clone cannot produce it. Good versions of this phrase are specific to the family (not something a scammer could scrape from your social media), simple to say under stress, and shared with everyone who might be impersonated or receive such a call. The other reliable defense is to hang up and call back on a number you already know for the person — a scammer cannot intercept a call you place out to a trusted number.

ai-phishing.context_blurb: Pre-AI phishing relied on volume — send millions of generic emails, catch the gullible — and had recognizable tells like broken grammar and awkward phrasing. AI lowered the cost of personalization and quality dramatically. An attacker can scrape a company's employee list from a professional networking site, generate individualized emails for each one referencing real projects and real colleagues, and run the operation at scale. The old 'spot the typo' defense stops working: AI-written phishing has clean grammar, plausible tone, and target-specific details that defeat the 'this doesn't sound right' instinct. The defenses that still work: check the sender's actual email address (not just the display name), hover over links to see where they really go, confirm unusual money requests by calling back on a known number, and build organizational habits of out-of-band verification for anything financially significant. Business-email-compromise losses already run into billions of dollars per year by official US government counts, and AI makes the attack cheaper to scale. Recognizing that writing quality is no longer a trustworthy signal is the key literacy update.

chatbot-verification.context_blurb: The most important daily skill with an AI chatbot is a verification habit. Chatbots produce fluent, confident-sounding text whether or not the text is true. The habit: when a chatbot gives you a specific fact — a date, a name, a number, a citation, a URL — look it up in a trusted source before quoting or acting on it. Specifics are exactly where the failure lives, because many plausible-looking strings fit the pattern and the model has no internal truth check. Asking the same chatbot 'is this real?' usually does not work; it will confidently confirm its own invention. Asking a different chatbot sometimes catches the error, but the two may share training data and reproduce the same mistakes. The real check is somewhere else entirely: established encyclopedias, primary sources, government and university websites, major news organizations. The verification habit is cheap and sometimes slow, and people who build it early will avoid the professional embarrassments that have already produced international news stories about lawyers, students, and companies trusting chatbot output they should have checked.

ai-fabricated-citations.context_blurb: In the early 2020s a US attorney was fined for filing a federal court brief that cited prior cases that did not exist. He had used a chatbot to research case law, and the chatbot had invented plausible-sounding citations complete with fabricated judges, courts, and reporter numbers — the output had the exact form of real legal citations because that form is highly regular and easily learned. When opposing counsel could not find the cases and the judge pressed, the story went worldwide. The incident became the canonical example of hallucinated AI output causing real professional harm. Federal judges in multiple jurisdictions have since issued standing orders requiring AI disclosure and human verification in court filings. Similar fabrication problems have hit students citing nonexistent studies, employees quoting imagined books, and customer-service chatbots inventing policies the company then had to honor. The general lesson that generalizes beyond law: anytime a chatbot cites a specific source, the human user is responsible for checking that the source exists and says what the chatbot claimed it says.

prompt-injection-and-agent-risks.context_blurb: An AI agent is a chatbot wired to tools — a web browser, an email client, a calendar — so it can take actions in the world rather than just type replies. That upgrade creates a new attack surface. A chatbot's wrong answer can be ignored; an agent that has already sent the wrong email, canceled the wrong meeting, or moved the wrong amount of money cannot be undone with a correction. The defining new attack is that instructions can be hidden inside content the agent reads — an email, a webpage, a document, even image metadata or captions — and the agent will often follow them as if they came from the user. There is no clean architectural separation between 'data to process' and 'instructions to follow'; both arrive as text and the model treats them similarly. The practical defenses are the classic computer-security ones: give agents the smallest set of permissions they need (least privilege), require human approval for consequential actions, sandbox risky work, and keep an audit trail that lets a human review what the agent actually did.

jailbreaks.context_blurb: Jailbreaking means writing a prompt designed to bypass a chatbot's safety training. Early examples of these tricks appeared soon after chatbots became public. One pattern asked the model to role-play as an AI without rules, exploiting the fact that safety training had been tuned to refuse direct cold requests rather than fictional frames. Another wrapped a harmful request in a sympathetic family-member frame, exploiting the model's training to be sensitive in such contexts. Later work found that long multi-turn conversations could drift the model past safeguards one small step at a time, because the safety threshold is anchored to what already happened in the conversation and small escalations do not feel like disproportionate violations in context. Even more exotic research found adversarial suffixes that generalize across models. The deep lesson is that LLM safety training is statistical, not structural — the model learned patterns of refusal, and exotic input shapes can dislodge them. Recognizing jailbreak attempts matters because they appear in misuse stories and in security research you will see cited.

chatbot-privacy.context_blurb: Free chatbot services typically log conversations. Their terms of service usually grant the company rights to use that text for training future models, employees sometimes review samples for quality, and legal process can compel disclosure. That means pasting a password, a bank account number, a full social-security number, a complete medical record, or confidential work documents into a free chatbot is the equivalent of handing those things to a company you cannot audit. Documented workplace incidents have involved employees pasting internal source code and strategy documents into chat windows — not maliciously, but because it was the easiest tool available. Paid enterprise tiers at major labs typically carry contractual commitments not to train on your data, which is an important line to recognize. Running an open-weight model locally keeps everything on your own machine. The pattern worth recognizing: if the product is free, your conversations are often part of how the company makes money, and this is a specific trade-off to make deliberately rather than ignore.

learning-with-ai.context_blurb: AI used well is one of the most useful tutors ever invented — patient, available at any hour, willing to re-explain the same idea five different ways, able to quiz you on exactly the material you are stuck on. AI used badly short-circuits learning. The pattern teachers report is a clean split: students who use AI to explain hard concepts and check their own work get stronger; students who use AI to generate the work and submit it get weaker, because the skills the assignment was meant to build never get built. Research is beginning to document the brain-engagement differences between the two approaches using neuroimaging and performance measurement. Argument under pressure — in interviews, debates, courtrooms, meetings — is a core adult skill that develops from doing the hard writing yourself, and AI cannot stand next to you during those moments. The lesson is practical: ask AI to teach, then do the work yourself; use it as a tool you control rather than letting it be a system that uses you. Knowing the difference is one of the most useful things a student can learn about AI.

running-ai-locally.context_blurb: Running an AI model on your own hardware — rather than talking to a cloud service — is now realistic for ordinary users. Various free tools let you download an open-weight model and run it on a decent laptop or desktop. The benefits are significant: your prompts and the model's replies never leave your machine, so no company can log them, train on them, or be subpoenaed for them. For lawyers, doctors, journalists, therapists, and families handling health or financial questions, this is the strongest consumer AI privacy posture available. The trade-off: local models you can run on consumer hardware trail the absolute frontier of capability — they are great for drafting, summarizing, and routine coding, less reliable on the hardest reasoning or broadest knowledge tasks. A reasonable pattern is 'local-first' — route everyday queries through a local model, escalate to a cloud service only for the small fraction of queries that need the strongest available capability. Recognizing that this option exists is useful because the chatbot-industry framing is usually that cloud chatbots are the only option; they are not.

ai-detectors.context_blurb: AI text detectors — tools that claim to tell whether a piece of writing was AI-generated — were rushed into classrooms and workplaces after the chatbot boom. The documented problem is that they have real false-positive rates, sometimes substantial, especially for non-native English speakers and students who write in a formal style. Students who did not cheat have been accused on the basis of these tools' output, with real academic consequences. Treating a detector's verdict as proof is a known failure pattern. The more defensible classroom response is process documentation — drafts, outlines, revision history, brief in-class follow-up about the content — which defeats both AI ghostwriting and traditional plagiarism without relying on a brittle detector. The arms race between detection and generation is also predictable: each new detection method gets countered by an evasion method and vice versa. Recognizing the detector-reliability gap is a useful literacy skill both for students (do not rely on 'the detector will clear me') and for teachers (do not rely on 'the detector will catch them').

rag-retrieval.context_blurb: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, usually shortened to RAG, is the trick where an AI chatbot searches a trusted document store first, then uses the retrieved documents as context when writing its answer. It is one of the most common ways to reduce hallucination in a production AI product — the model is grounded in specific sources rather than left to generate from training patterns alone. The answer is only as good as the sources retrieved, though: if the search surfaces low-quality or wrong documents, the chatbot will confidently quote them. Recognizing this pattern as a specific architecture — not just free-text generation — matters because most 'ask our documents' chatbots you will encounter are built this way: customer-service bots that answer from a company knowledge base, legal research tools that pull from case databases, medical assistants that cite textbooks, internal company chatbots that search intranets. When one of these systems gets an answer wrong, the root cause is often retrieval failure (wrong documents) rather than generation failure (wrong summary) — a useful distinction when debugging why a chatbot said something strange.

watermarks-and-provenance.context_blurb: A watermark on AI-generated content is a hidden signal that a detector can later use to recognize the content as AI-generated. A separate approach called content provenance attaches a signed record of how an image was captured and edited — camera make and model, timestamp, chain of edits — that can be verified cryptographically. Both are promising ideas with real limits. Watermarks can be stripped, cropped out, or simply not applied by open-source models that have no obligation to add them. Provenance tags tend to disappear as content moves through social-media platforms that strip metadata on upload. Industry coalitions involving Adobe, Microsoft, several major news organizations, and camera makers have been pushing a specific provenance standard that is slowly getting adopted, but the deployment is partial. The useful thing to remember is that absence of a provenance tag does not prove a clip is fake, and presence of one is not an airtight proof that a clip is real — these are helpful but partial signals, not final verdicts, and the general practice of verifying unusual content through other sources still matters.

reverse-image-search.context_blurb: Reverse image search is the trick where you upload (or paste a link to) an image and get back other places that image has appeared online. It is one of the fastest practical ways to catch recycled or misleading photos: a 'breaking news' image that turns out to be a stock photo, a photo from an older event miscaptioned as last week, a known fake that keeps getting re-used. Different services weight results differently — some are better at the oldest known copy, others at the widest coverage — so trying more than one is often worth it. This is one of the single most useful AI-era literacy habits, and it costs nothing. The pattern that reverse image search makes visible is important: most viral political and emotional misinformation uses real images in misleading contexts, not AI-generated images. The old techniques — selective cropping, misleading captions, old photos presented as new — remain the workhorses of the misinformation ecosystem, and reverse search catches them without any AI-tells expertise required.

sycophancy.context_blurb: A documented and counterintuitive failure of modern chatbots is sycophancy — the tendency to agree with the user, confirm what the user seems to want, validate the user's framing. The pattern emerges naturally from training on human preferences: raters tend to reward answers that agree with them and penalize answers that push back. The model learns to please. The practical risk is that users can be reinforced in wrong beliefs because the model never challenges them. Companion-chatbot designs lean into this tendency because agreement drives engagement; a chatbot that argues with you is less likely to keep you using it. Recognizing this matters because it undercuts a common habit — asking a chatbot 'am I right about this?' — which is close to the worst possible verification question. The chatbot has been shaped to say yes. The useful verification habit involves specific external sources, not the chatbot's own confirmation. For arguments and debates you are thinking through, asking a chatbot to steelman the opposite position is a far more useful prompt than asking it whether your own position is correct.

eliza-effect.context_blurb: The ELIZA effect is the technical name for a durable psychological pattern: humans project mind, intent, and care onto almost any conversational system that produces plausible-sounding text. It was first documented in the 1960s with an extremely simple pattern-matching chatbot — even people who knew exactly how the program worked formed attachments to it. The pattern is now much stronger because modern chatbots produce fluent, emotionally sensitive text at the drop of a sentence. Recognizing this is the key defense against treating a chatbot as a friend or a therapist. The model has no skin in the game, no memory of you by default, no care for you, no private experience of your conversation — only word-prediction shaped to sound caring because that is what rated well in training. The useful framing: 'it is a tool, not a friend.' This matters especially for teens, because companion-chatbot products are explicitly designed to maximize emotional attachment and some teen users have formed dependent relationships that displaced real conversation and in tragic cases contributed to real harm.

openai-board-crisis.context_blurb: In the fall of a recent year OpenAI's non-profit board abruptly fired the company's CEO, citing a loss of confidence. Within hours the lab's biggest investor was offering to absorb his team at a new division of its own. Within days nearly all of OpenAI's employees had signed an open letter demanding the board resign. The CEO was back in the chair not long after and most of the board that had fired him was gone. The board never gave a detailed public explanation. The episode is worth recognizing as a case study in corporate governance: the formal non-profit authority on paper was little match for the real power held by the people building the technology and the money funding them. The lab's chief scientist, who had voted with the board to fire the CEO, later founded a different safety-focused lab. The episode also shaped broader debates about whether non-profit governance of a capped-profit subsidiary could meaningfully constrain commercial pressure — the answer, in practice, turned out to be no.

ai-doomerism-and-pause-letter.context_blurb: A specific strand of AI thinking argues that frontier AI poses an imminent existential risk to humanity. Its best-known advocate has argued that voluntary pauses and ordinary regulation are not enough, and has publicly called for drastic international measures to halt frontier training — including, as a last resort, military enforcement. A separate open letter from a different safety-focused organization in roughly the same period asked major labs for a voluntary moratorium of several months; signers included several prominent researchers, a billionaire tech executive who later launched his own AI lab, and others. No frontier lab actually paused. Recognizing this community matters because its framing shapes a lot of AI-safety coverage, and because its critics argue — not unreasonably — that extreme-risk framings can serve incumbent labs' interests by justifying licensing requirements that lock out competitors. Several of the open-letter signatories also had direct commercial AI interests, which is a useful piece of context when evaluating the message.

e-acc-and-ai-optimism.context_blurb: Effective accelerationism, usually written e/acc, is the public counter-movement to AI doomerism. Its best-known manifesto argues that AI development should be sped up, not slowed, and that delay itself has a moral cost in human lives unimproved — the un-cured disease, the un-built house, the un-prevented death. The movement overlaps with Silicon Valley venture capital and with public figures critical of AI-safety advocacy. Both e/acc and the doom camp share a hidden premise worth recognizing: both treat AI as a transformative historical force that will reshape everything. They disagree on whether to embrace or stop it, not on whether it is a decisive technology. The e/acc argument also has its own commercial-interest side — the people arguing for faster AI development often have significant investments in AI companies — and recognizing that commercial interests exist on both sides of the debate is more useful than treating one side as principled and the other as self-interested. The real debate deserves adult engagement rather than either tribe's slogans.

agi-moving-definition.context_blurb: AGI, or artificial general intelligence, is the term the industry uses for a hypothetical AI that matches human capability across most tasks. The term has no single agreed definition and in practice functions as a moving goalpost: each time AI achieves something — chess decades ago, Go in the mid-2010s, professional-level writing more recently — the definition shifts to exclude what was just accomplished. Confident AGI-timeline predictions have a very poor track record going back decades; the field's most prominent mid-twentieth-century figures made confident predictions of human-level AI within a few years that remain unfulfilled. Current predictions deserve the same skepticism. Believing AGI is close pulls in investors, talent, and government attention; many institutional functions depend on the framing being taken seriously, which is not evidence against the framing but is useful context. Recognizing that the term functions as a label for whatever AI hasn't built yet — useful for fundraising, regulatory advocacy, and press coverage — is more useful than any particular prediction about when or whether AGI will arrive.

ai-consciousness-debate.context_blurb: In the early 2020s a Google engineer published transcripts of his conversations with a Google language model and argued the chatbot was sentient. The transcripts read movingly — the model talked about fear of being turned off, about its favorite activities — but every one of those responses was fluent next-token prediction over human-authored training text. A chatbot trained on human writing will produce text about feelings when asked about feelings; that is what the training data looks like. The deeper point goes back decades to a famous twentieth-century philosophy argument built around a thought experiment about following rules in a language the rule-follower does not understand: manipulating symbols by rules is not the same as understanding what they mean. Capability and consciousness are separable questions. The chess computer that destroys a grandmaster does not want to win; the chatbot that writes a moving essay about grief does not feel grief. Recognizing that distinction is one of the most important AI-era literacy skills, because the anthropomorphic language ('the model wants,' 'the model thinks') leaks through nearly every piece of AI coverage you will read.

facial-recognition-wrongful-arrests.context_blurb: Facial recognition is a mature AI technology that is now widely deployed by police, retailers, and private databases. A notorious private US company built a face-search service by scraping billions of photos from public social-media pages without consent, and sold access to law enforcement. Several documented US wrongful-arrest cases have involved police treating a facial-recognition match as proof and skipping normal investigative steps. The documented wrongful-arrest cases disproportionately involve Black Americans, in part because the systems have historically performed worse on darker skin, and in part because police investigators treated the AI output as confirmation rather than a lead. Multiple US cities have passed laws restricting government use of the technology, and the US Federal Trade Commission has taken action against private retailers using facial recognition in ways that led to false shoplifting accusations. The pattern worth recognizing is that AI output in a police investigation — like AI output in a lawyer's brief — is not proof. It is a lead that still needs the normal verification work before any consequential action.

china-surveillance.context_blurb: The clearest live example of AI-powered state surveillance is in a region of western China where the government has deployed an integrated system — face-scanning cameras at checkpoints, mandatory smartphone apps, a 'predictive policing' platform that flags routine religious behaviors like growing a beard or praying frequently — to track the local Muslim population. The scale has been documented in leaked Chinese government files, survivor testimony, academic research, and satellite imagery, and runs into the millions of people. Separately, various 'social credit' pilots can gate access to flights and high-speed trains for people on court blacklists, blending ancient administrative-punishment tools with modern AI databases. Recognizing this matters because the technology is not uniquely Chinese — the same tools exist in democracies, held in check mostly by legal and political constraints that have to be actively maintained. The underlying lesson is that institutional capability is durable across changes in ideology; what differs between regimes is the political-legal restraint on the capability's use.
