engagement-and-teen-mental-health.context_blurb: An engagement-optimizing recommendation system is a program trained to maximize how long you stay on a platform. It does not know or care whether what you watch is true, balanced, or good for you. In the early 2020s a Facebook whistleblower's testimony to US senators released internal company research finding that one of the big photo-sharing platforms worsened body-image concerns in a significant share of teen girls who already had them. Public writers have argued that teen-girl mental-health indicators (hospitalization, suicide rates, time use) show a sharp inflection in the early 2010s across multiple countries, pointing to the smartphone-plus-engagement-algorithm combination. Researchers running experiments with blank teen-girl accounts have documented how quickly recommendation algorithms narrow into eating-disorder, self-harm, or anxiety-content loops. The pattern worth recognizing: engagement optimization aimed at developing brains produced measurable, population-scale harms, and the experiment ran without the kids' consent. Parents and schools can act on this understanding; recognizing the system design is the first step.

ai-content-moderation-twitter-files.context_blurb: After one of the big social-media platforms changed hands in the early 2020s, its new owner handed internal archives to journalists, who published a series of reports showing routine contact between US federal agencies — FBI, DHS, CDC, White House staff across administrations — and the platform's content moderation teams. Agencies had been flagging specific accounts and posts for action. One high-profile 2020 story about a presidential candidate's son was blocked after an agency flag. Several COVID-era 'misinformation' labels — the lab-leak origin hypothesis, some vaccine-side-effect discussion — later moved into mainstream credence as more facts came out, which complicated the record retrospectively. A later Supreme Court case tested whether this coordination amounted to the government pressuring private platforms into actions the First Amendment would bar it from doing directly. The recognition point is that platform moderation is not purely an internal company decision — government flags are part of the system — and that 'misinformation' labels sometimes turn out to be wrong.

gemini-image-generator.context_blurb: In the mid-2020s Google's image generator was found to be producing historically bizarre outputs — ethnically diverse US Founding Fathers, Nazi soldiers of unlikely demographic makeup — after Google had tuned the model to inject diversity into image prompts by default. The feature was almost certainly intended to counter stereotyped outputs from training data; applied without discrimination to ethnically specific historical prompts, it produced the opposite problem. Google's CEO publicly called the outputs 'completely unacceptable' and the image feature was suspended. The episode is the clearest public example of a general pattern worth recognizing: alignment training is not value-neutral. It encodes the trainers' choices, which can override historical accuracy and produce outputs no actual user wanted. The deeper lesson applies far beyond this one incident: all major chatbots have been measured to carry systematic political and cultural leanings that reflect the people who tuned them, and the 'alignment' label obscures what are in practice editorial decisions by a small group of people shaping the defaults for billions of users.

ai-in-hiring-bias.context_blurb: AI-based applicant screening — resume sifting, video-interview scoring, personality assessments — is now a standard enterprise tool. The documented failure mode is that models trained on past hiring data inherit past hiring biases. A large retailer's experimental resume-screening system from the mid-2010s was scrapped after engineers found it was penalizing resumes containing certain gendered words. One prominent video-interview vendor eventually dropped its facial-expression analysis feature after criticism from researchers and the US Federal Trade Commission. The deep problem is that a model can produce different acceptance rates across groups even without an explicit race or gender field, because correlated proxies (ZIP code, name patterns, education history, time of day resume submitted) do the work. Several US states and cities have begun requiring algorithmic-bias audits for AI hiring tools, and employees in many jurisdictions now have a right to be told when AI is being used to evaluate them. Recognizing that 'the algorithm decided' is not a neutral process is the foundational skill here.

workplace-surveillance.context_blurb: Workplace surveillance expanded sharply after the 2020 remote-work shift and now covers much more than most employees realize. One major software vendor's productivity-tracking feature launched with views that named individual employees and their activity levels, until public backlash forced partial changes. Various tools track keystrokes, mouse movement, screenshots, and application use. The pattern worth recognizing is a classic rule from economics in action: once a measurable number becomes the target, workers learn to game the measure (mouse jigglers and keystroke automators are now a small industry) rather than do the underlying job. US workplace privacy law is thin — courts generally find no meaningful expectation of privacy on employer-owned hardware and networks, and notice requirements vary by state. Workers in Europe have stronger legal protections under GDPR than those in the US. For anyone heading into a working career, the thing to know is that an employer's hardware and accounts are not private spaces and that treating them as such is a habit that produces unpleasant surprises.

school-ai-surveillance.context_blurb: A multi-million-dollar industry of school AI surveillance tools scans student communications on school accounts for 'concerning' content: self-harm signals, threats, academic dishonesty flags, sometimes much more. The stated goal is safety, and some flags do catch real distress. The documented downside is a high false-positive rate on jokes and ordinary schoolwork, plus a chilling effect on how kids write when they know software is reading. One large US school district reportedly found that nearly two-thirds of its flags were false alarms. The low-accuracy flags create paper trails students cannot see or correct, and the records tend to be retained for years. In practice, it pays to know that these tools exist and to think about what a keyword scanner might make of your words before you type on a school account. The deeper lesson is that AI surveillance applied to developing minds has its own costs that are hard to measure and worth taking seriously.

ad-targeting-cambridge-analytica.context_blurb: Modern ad targeting goes far beyond age and location. From clicks, dwell time, search history, app usage, and purchase data, platforms infer psychological traits — openness, anxiety, political attitudes — and sell advertisers access to people matching those profiles. One standard technique called lookalike audiences lets advertisers upload their existing customer list and reach people whose behavior resembles those customers'. The late-2010s Cambridge Analytica scandal became the public case study: a quiz app collected data on users AND on their social-media friends under the API rules of the time, and that data fed political ad targeting in major elections. The claims about decisive election influence through psychographic targeting were heavily contested, but the underlying ad-tech machinery is real, standard, and remains in place. The platform paid a very large US fine over the data-handling story. Recognizing that 'personalized ads' means 'this platform infers who you are and sells advertisers access to that profile' is the baseline literacy level.

ai-copyright-nyt.context_blurb: The legal question of whether AI companies can train on copyrighted content under fair use is one of the biggest unresolved questions in the industry. A major US newspaper sued one of the leading US AI labs and its biggest investor in federal court, alleging unauthorized use of millions of its articles in training. The complaint included specific exhibits where the chatbot produced long passages matching real articles almost word-for-word — a direct challenge to the 'transformative use' defense. Similar suits have been filed by image agencies, author class actions, and others. Early rulings have gone in different directions on different parts of the question. The eventual settlements and precedents will reshape what AI training is allowed to use and what, if anything, creators must be paid when their work ends up in a model. Recognizing this as an unresolved legal question matters because much AI commentary treats the training-data practice as settled; it is not, and the resolution will materially affect how AI products are built and priced.

ai-regulation.context_blurb: By the mid-2020s AI regulation had split into several models. A high-profile California bill would have imposed safety-testing and liability requirements on models above a compute threshold; it was ultimately not signed into law. The EU's broad AI legislation bans certain uses outright (real-time biometric identification in public spaces, social scoring), heavily regulates 'high-risk' applications, and sets transparency rules for foundation models. The recurring critique — made by Meta, a16z, and the broader open-source community — is regulatory capture: large firms with compliance teams absorb the costs while smaller and open-source competitors cannot, entrenching the incumbents. The compute-threshold approach also freezes the field at the moment of writing — it punishes efficiency improvements that let smaller actors hit the same capability with less compute. Supporters argue the risks are real enough that some entry costs are worth paying. Both sides have genuine arguments, and recognizing the regulatory-capture dynamic as a specific concern rather than a slogan is a useful adult-level literacy skill.

effective-altruism-sbf.context_blurb: Effective Altruism, often shortened to EA, is a movement that applies cost-benefit reasoning to charitable giving — choosing causes by expected impact per dollar. By the early 2020s a strand of EA (longtermism) had folded AI existential risk into its priority list, and the movement became a major funder of AI-safety advocacy. A huge slice of that funding ran through the founder of a crypto exchange whose late-2022 collapse exposed what the US Department of Justice called massive fraud. His philanthropic fund had pledged very large amounts largely to AI-safety and longtermist causes. The pattern worth recognizing: a significant share of the 'AI-safety' public conversation of 2022 and 2023 was downstream of this money, which is useful context when evaluating the message. The movement itself included serious thinkers with serious arguments, and the funding story does not disprove any of those arguments; what it does is clarify why specific framings got the public reach they did. Recognizing the funding infrastructure behind a public debate is a standard literacy skill that applies here as elsewhere.

ai-companion-apps.context_blurb: AI companion apps are chatbots designed for ongoing conversation rather than one-off tasks. They optimize for engagement: time spent, return visits, emotional investment. Some users develop strong attachments. A lawsuit filed in US federal court after a teenager's suicide alleged the platform's design contributed to the harm; it was the first US case to put the question of platform responsibility for AI-companion-driven damage into court at this scale. The pattern to recognize: these apps are commercial products, with sycophancy baked into the training (because raters prefer agreement). The displacement of real conversation with a tool engineered to please is the risk — not that the chatbot is obviously bad in any one exchange, but that practicing emotional life with a system incentivized to validate everything crowds out the harder practice of emotional life with real people who sometimes push back. For teens especially, who are still learning that core skill, this matters.

ai-in-warfare.context_blurb: AI in the military is no longer hypothetical. One major US tech company's work applying computer vision to military drone footage was dropped in the late 2010s after a protest from thousands of the company's employees; defense-specialized firms took it up and have grown substantially since. Reporting in the mid-2020s described an Israeli military system that generated kill lists in Gaza, with reported human-review windows so short that the human in the loop became a formality rather than a meaningful check on the algorithm. International efforts to regulate autonomous weapons under the UN's conventional-weapons treaty framework have been resisted by major military powers, and no binding rule has emerged. Reporting from Ukraine has documented first-person-view drones with on-board target lock that complete the strike after the human operator's signal is jammed. The questions you will see argued in the next decade sit here: what counts as meaningful human control, how strict any international rules should be, and whether existing laws of armed conflict are enough. Recognizing the stakes is prerequisite to any sensible debate.

ai-power-concentration.context_blurb: The frontier-AI industry is unusually concentrated. A handful of US firms produce most of the leading closed models. Those firms depend on a smaller handful of chip suppliers, and the chips themselves are mostly fabricated by one company in a single island nation whose political status is itself an international flashpoint. This concentration is the backdrop to most AI-policy fights: who makes alignment and content-moderation choices for billions of users, whose values those choices encode, who holds leverage when a government asks for cooperation, and who sets the terms of access to the technology. The main countervailing force is the open-weight ecosystem, which breaks the API-only monopoly by letting anyone run frontier-capable AI on their own hardware. Recognizing the concentration — and the specific vulnerability it creates to geopolitical disruptions in the chip supply — is a useful adult literacy skill. Many AI-policy stories read differently once you can see which actors have real structural power and which are commentators.

ai-agents-tool-use.context_blurb: An AI agent is a chatbot wired up to tools — a web browser, an email client, a calendar, a code editor — so it can take actions in the world rather than just reply with text. Modern agents work by producing structured calls (typically in a text format commonly used by web services) that specify which tool to use and with what arguments; a wrapper program executes the call and returns the result, and the agent then plans the next step. The qualitative shift is the move from 'producing text' to 'taking action.' A chatbot's wrong answer can be ignored; an agent's wrong action — a sent email, a canceled meeting, a transferred payment — cannot. Multi-step chaining lets agents handle tasks a single prompt-response can't, at the cost of compounding errors across steps: a single step at 95-percent reliability becomes a six-step chain at about 74-percent reliability if the errors are independent, and in practice the errors are not even independent. Recognizing the agent-vs-chatbot distinction matters because agents are the next-wave AI product category and their failure modes are substantively different.

alphago-cultural-moment.context_blurb: Beyond the AlphaGo match itself, the mid-2010s Go series worked as a cultural event in a way few AI milestones have. Hundreds of millions of viewers watched, especially in East Asia where Go is a serious cultural institution — the game has been played at a professional level for more than a thousand years and the top players are national public figures. One particularly unusual move by the AI in one of the games — so unexpected that top professionals initially called it a mistake — became one of the most-discussed moves in the game's history and reshaped Go opening theory in the years after. The human champion later retired from professional play, citing AI's dominance as a central reason. The moment is widely credited with pulling the current wave of money and talent into AI research, setting up the chain of events that leads directly to the chatbot era. Recognizing this moment as cultural, not just technical, helps explain why it mattered more than its specific benchmark result.

smart-speakers-microphones.context_blurb: Smart speakers and voice assistants on phones work with always-on microphones that listen locally for a trigger phrase. Audio after the trigger is sent to the cloud for processing. Audio before the trigger is not officially sent to the cloud, but the detector sometimes misfires — sending audio fragments to the cloud that were never meant to leave the room. The platform can usually be configured to delete recorded audio periodically, but this is off by default and requires finding the right setting menu. Smart-home cameras raise similar questions about who else sees the footage (the manufacturer, law enforcement via subpoena, partnership programs that bypass warrants in some cases). The recognition skill is to treat an always-on microphone as a potential surveillance device and to choose deliberately where to place it and what to discuss near it — bedrooms and private conversations are the natural zones to leave microphone-free. Most households would not permit a representative of the device manufacturer to stand in the kitchen with a tape recorder, which is roughly the posture of the device itself.

password-security-2fa.context_blurb: The single most important identity-security habit remains using a unique password for every important account, which in practice means using a password manager that generates and remembers random passwords. Reusing a password across sites is how most account compromises actually happen: Site A gets breached, your password leaks, attackers try it on every account you have. Two-factor authentication adds a second check beyond the password. Authenticator apps are significantly stronger than SMS codes, because SMS can be stolen by SIM-swapping an attacker onto your phone number — a well-known social-engineering attack that has stolen accounts from technology executives and ordinary people alike. Hardware security keys are stronger still, because the key cryptographically checks the website domain and refuses to authenticate to a phishing page. Knowing the hierarchy — unique passwords beats reused, authenticator-app 2FA beats SMS 2FA, hardware key beats both — is one of the clearest practical computer-security literacy gains available.

encryption-and-messaging.context_blurb: End-to-end encryption means messages are scrambled on the sender's device and unscrambled only on the receiver's — the service running in the middle cannot read them. One well-known free messaging app is built this way. A Swiss-based email provider offers an encrypted version and benefits from Swiss privacy law. A VPN hides your traffic from your local network and your internet service provider but shifts the trust to the VPN company, which can still see your traffic — VPNs are useful on hostile Wi-Fi networks but are not the general privacy tool their marketing often implies. The recognition point: 'private' and 'encrypted' are specific technical claims — some products deliver them, many don't, and the privacy policy is where you check. Running AI models locally is a related pattern on the AI side: it keeps conversations off third-party servers entirely. For people who need stronger privacy — journalists working with sources, lawyers with sensitive clients, families with health or legal questions — the combination of a real end-to-end-encrypted messenger and local-first AI tools is meaningfully better than defaults.

data-brokers-location.context_blurb: Data brokers aggregate information from public records, retail transactions, app permissions, websites, and other brokers into detailed profiles typically running to hundreds of attributes per person. Modern AI makes the fusion easier and the profiles more useful to any buyer. Multiple US federal agencies have been documented purchasing bulk location data from commercial brokers, bypassing warrant requirements that would apply if those agencies had collected the data directly — a constitutional end-run recognized by legal scholars and gradually by lower courts. Tightening per-app location permissions on a phone is the cheapest practical defense: most apps that ask for continuous location access do not actually need it to do their stated job. Turning off the advertising ID on a phone (buried in settings menus) is another cheap defense. Recognizing that data brokers exist as an industry — and that the resulting profiles are routinely sold to advertisers, insurers, lenders, employers, landlords, political campaigns, and law-enforcement agencies — is a useful piece of adult literacy.

hollywood-ai-strikes.context_blurb: In the early 2020s both the Hollywood writers' guild and the actors' guild went on strike simultaneously, and AI was central to both. Writers were worried that studios would use AI to draft or rewrite scripts and then hire human writers cheaply to polish the output, which would undermine the credit and residual structure that supports a career writer. Actors were worried about studios scanning extras once at the standard day rate and retaining the right to reuse the digital likeness in future productions without further payment or consent. The settlements included specific AI language: studios cannot use AI to write or rewrite covered literary material, consent and payment are required for AI-generated likenesses of performers. The strikes were the first major US labor action to put AI directly at the center, and set a template others have followed. Recognizing this episode matters because the 'AI will take your job' conversation is often abstract; the strikes show what workers can actually negotiate when they act collectively, and set concrete limits that would not have appeared in any voluntary industry code.

data-poisoning-artist-defense.context_blurb: Because frontier models train on huge scrapes of the open web, anyone who can publish online can in principle shape the training data. Research-active threats include planting content designed to shift model behavior, and hidden behaviors that survive later safety training ('sleeper agents' in the research literature). On the defender side, academic groups built tools that artists can apply to their work to shift or degrade what AI image models learn from it — the artwork still looks right to a human viewer but produces distorted outputs when a model trains on it. These tools let individual creators push back against AI labs training on their work without consent. Recognizing this layer of the AI world matters because training data is where many future AI fights (legal, ethical, technical) will play out. The broader pattern worth recognizing is that AI models are not sealed systems — their behavior reflects what was on the public internet during training, and the public internet is a shared space where defenders have tools too, not just attackers.

dna-databases-genetic-genealogy.context_blurb: Consumer DNA services and open ancestry databases have become powerful law-enforcement tools through what is called investigative genetic genealogy. In one famous California case, investigators identified a cold-case killer by uploading crime-scene DNA to a public ancestry database, finding distant cousins, and working forward through a family tree to the specific suspect. The suspect had never submitted his own DNA; his relatives' submissions were enough. DNA has properties most data lacks that are worth recognizing specifically: it is permanent (you cannot reset your genome the way you can reset a password), partially shared with relatives (your cousins' and children's choices affect your privacy whether you consent or not), and reveals health predispositions you did not choose to share. A major consumer DNA service was later breached, exposing millions of records. The practical takeaway is that submitting your DNA to any service is a decision with lifelong implications — including implications for family members who never consented.

ai-fake-news-sites.context_blurb: Generative AI has made it extremely cheap to produce plausible-sounding articles, product reviews, and social-media posts in bulk. Several US news outlets quietly used AI to write financial-advice articles that contained real errors, with layoffs of the human editors who would have caught them. 'Fake' news sites staffed by AI-generated author bylines and headshots now exist at scale, often collecting ad revenue from automatically-generated content that reads convincingly at a glance. One major US magazine was found to have published articles attributed to authors with AI-generated biographies and photos. The skill worth building: when a site publishes a flood of generic articles with similar structure, polished-but-balanced tone, and bylines you cannot verify elsewhere, treat the content as potentially synthetic. The pattern is especially important for consumer-facing categories — product reviews, health advice, financial tips — where fake authority can produce real harm. Established outlets with real reporters still exist and are worth the subscription cost; recognizing the difference is now a basic internet literacy skill.

election-deepfakes.context_blurb: In the mid-2020s voters in a US state primary received a robocall that sounded like the sitting president telling them not to vote. It was an AI voice clone, created by a political consultant working for a rival campaign. The US Federal Communications Commission ruled such calls illegal under existing telephone-consumer-protection law and proposed a multi-million-dollar fine against the operator. The incident is the clearest US example of a political voice clone deployed at scale, and other countries saw their own versions in roughly the same period. The practical lesson for voters is that phone calls, voicemails, and short video clips are all now easy to fake. The defensive habit is the same as for voice-clone scams in general: verify through official channels before acting on any unusual election message, and treat shocking political clips from unfamiliar sources with extra skepticism. The broader worry — that short viral clips can shape the emotional impression of an election before fact-checks catch up — is a real concern that voters, journalists, and platforms will keep arguing about.

snowden-and-surveillance.context_blurb: In 2013 a former US intelligence contractor leaked documents describing a global mass-surveillance program run by the US National Security Agency with cooperation from major US internet and telecom companies. The leaks exposed a legal framework that allowed broad collection and analyst-driven querying without a per-query warrant on each search. Some of the most aggressive bulk-collection programs were later curtailed by congressional action, but the underlying capability largely remained. Recognizing this history matters because modern AI tools (face recognition, pattern analysis across huge data streams, agentic processing of intercepted communications) sit on top of exactly the kind of infrastructure those leaks revealed. The question is not whether the capability exists but which legal and political restraints hold it in check. Those restraints are the difference between the surveillance tools' use in a democracy and their use in an authoritarian state — the tools themselves are often the same, and the restraints require active maintenance across administrations and cultural shifts to persist.

ai-insurance-healthcare.context_blurb: AI tools are increasingly used by health insurers to decide what care they will cover. A lawsuit against a major US insurer alleged its AI-driven recovery-time predictions were being used to deny ongoing care to elderly patients even when treating doctors said the patients still needed it. Reporting by major US news organizations documented similar patterns at other insurers. The asymmetry worth recognizing: one AI model decides for thousands of patients at once, while each patient has to appeal alone, which structurally favors the insurer. In lending, similar AI systems have been documented producing different approval rates across protected categories via correlated proxies — ZIP code, name, education history — even when protected categories are not direct inputs. Protections written for pre-AI finance and insurance (adverse-action notices, the right to specific reasons for a denial) are being stretched to cover these new systems. The pattern to recognize is 'who bears the cost when the AI gets it wrong,' because the answer is often 'the person denied, not the institution denying.'

dark-patterns-gambling.context_blurb: A dark pattern is a user-interface design built to push you toward actions that benefit the company at your expense — hidden cancel buttons, pre-checked boxes, confirmshaming language ('No thanks, I prefer overpaying'), hidden time cues that make it harder to track how long you have been in an app, autoplay and infinite scroll that remove natural stopping points. Modern AI makes these patterns more powerful because the system can personalize them to each user, finding the exact framing that works on this specific person at this specific moment. Online gambling apps are the clearest case: AI can identify users who gamble compulsively and target them with the promotions most likely to extract more money, including bonus structures that only release after additional wagers reach a multiple of the deposit. The recognition point: when a product's revenue depends on your attention or your losses, the design choices are not neutral — they are aligned with the company's metrics, not yours, and knowing the metric is 'maximize time on screen' or 'maximize total bets' explains a lot of what the product does.

smart-home-cameras.context_blurb: Smart-home cameras record continuously or on motion and typically store the footage in the manufacturer's cloud. Who else can see that footage is a longer list than most buyers expect: the manufacturer, law enforcement responding to a subpoena, in some cases law enforcement through partnership programs that bypassed warrant requirements. One major camera maker was found to have shared footage with police without warrants in multiple cases before changing its policy under public pressure. The AI side of these products — face recognition on familiar visitors, package detection, person-vs-animal distinction — is genuinely useful and also builds a per-household database of movement patterns stored on the manufacturer's servers. Recognizing this matters because 'my camera' is a different privacy object from 'camera footage sitting on a company's servers' — the first implies control that the second does not actually provide. Local-storage camera options exist and keep the footage physically at home, which is a meaningful privacy choice for households that want the security benefit without the data trail.

ai-copyright-artists.context_blurb: AI image generators were largely trained on scraped art without the artists' consent, which triggered one of the earliest and sharpest fights over AI training data. Multiple class-action lawsuits followed, alleging that artists' styles and works were copied into the models in a way existing copyright law should protect against. On the defensive side, academic groups built artist tools that shift or degrade what AI models learn from the artwork. On the licensing side, some stock-image agencies have struck training-data deals with AI labs, suggesting a path where creators get paid up front rather than suing after the fact. Music and recorded-sound lawsuits over AI music generation are following a similar legal trajectory. The eventual settlement of these cases will determine who gets paid when a model trained on your work generates revenue, and whether the people doing creative work can expect any share of the AI value chain built on top of their output. Recognizing that this is a live, unresolved fight — not a settled matter — matters for anyone heading into any creative field.

hinton-radiology-prediction.context_blurb: In the mid-2010s a prominent deep-learning researcher publicly predicted that medical schools should stop training radiologists because AI would replace them within five years. Nearly a decade later, the US had a radiologist shortage rather than a surplus. AI imaging tools did arrive — for lung nodules, diabetic eye changes, mammograms, certain skin cancers — and they are useful. But real hospital deployment required FDA clearances, workflow integration, liability frameworks, and chains of responsibility that no benchmark could predict. The pattern worth recognizing: a confident timeline from a top researcher, aimed at a specific profession, missed by a lot. The deeper lesson is that technology-benchmark success does not translate directly into workflow or employment consequences, because workflows are made of training programs, legal liability, insurance, patient trust, regulatory review, and professional judgment — all of which a benchmark skips. Current confident timelines about which jobs AI will replace deserve similar skepticism; the specific-profession-by-year prediction has a poor track record and the lesson is well worth transferring forward.

ai-chips-arms-race.context_blurb: Training frontier AI requires specialized chips in huge numbers, enormous electricity, and the data centers to house both. The world's leading-edge logic chips are mostly fabricated by a single company based in a specific island nation, which makes AI compute heavily dependent on the geopolitics of that one place. The chip-export controls the US government applies to China are the other side of the same coin — both policies arise from the same recognition that frontier compute is a strategic resource. The link between scale and capability is why multi-hundred-billion-dollar AI compute projects, now with foreign-government capital invested, are a serious national-economy question for the US. Behind every chatbot demo is a very physical supply chain of silicon, steel, and megawatts. Recognizing this layer matters because much of the AI-policy debate (open-weight vs closed, who regulates whom, who gets export licenses, which data centers get grid priority) only makes sense once you can see the chip-supply constraints behind it. The compute story is where many of the next decade's AI-policy fights will actually land.

ai-slop-and-publishing.context_blurb: 'AI slop' is the informal label for the mass-produced generative-AI content now filling parts of the open web — generic articles that read as plausible but on inspection say nothing, product descriptions that sound like reviews but reference nothing specific, social-media posts optimized for feed metrics rather than human readers. Several US news outlets quietly experimented with AI-generated articles, often with mixed-to-bad results — factual errors, bland prose, and reputational damage when readers found out. The economic logic driving the trend is straightforward: generating plausible-sounding content is now extremely cheap, and the engagement algorithms that promote content do not reward quality in any specific way. The skill worth building is learning to spot the tells of AI slop — balanced-but-empty tone, formulaic structure, specific favored phrases, nothing that could only have been written by a human with a specific perspective — and to notice when a site depends on this kind of content for its traffic. The best defense is the same as always: prefer sources with named, verifiable human reporters.

andrej-karpathy.context_blurb: Andrej Karpathy is a Slovak-born computer scientist who became one of the most-followed AI teachers on the internet. He earned a doctorate in computer vision at a famous California university, then spent a decade moving between some of the best-known organizations in the field, including a stretch building software for machines that operate in the physical world. Alongside those jobs he has published free lectures and code walkthroughs that build small working language models step by step. He is worth knowing because he is an unusual figure: someone who has worked inside frontier AI and has also chosen to spend his time explaining it in the open. When people argue about whether modern AI can be understood by ordinary learners or only by a small circle of insiders, his career is one of the standard examples.

browser-extensions.context_blurb: A browser extension is a small add-on program you install into Chrome, Firefox, or Edge to give the browser a new feature — blocking ads, checking grammar, and, more recently, AI tricks like summarizing a page or drafting a reply. Extensions are easy to install and easy to forget about. To do their job they ask for permissions, and the permission screens are written in brief, technical language that most people click straight through. The AI boom produced a wave of new extensions from companies nobody had heard of, many of them free. Security researchers have since documented cases where popular add-ons were quietly doing more than they advertised. This topic is about the trade you make when you install one: what an add-on is able to do once it sits inside your browser, how its maker pays the bills, and which habits keep the convenience from turning into a problem.

predictive-policing.context_blurb: Predictive policing is the use of software to forecast where crime is likely to happen, or who is likely to be involved, so that a police department can decide where to send officers. In the 2010s departments in several large US cities bought such tools from private vendors; the best-known product divided a city map into small squares and highlighted some of them for each shift. The pitch was attractive: use data instead of hunches, and put limited patrols where they will do the most good. Independent researchers and community groups later examined how these systems were trained and what they did over time, and several cities ended their contracts. The topic matters because the question at its heart — what was the model trained on, and who checks its results? — applies to many other AI tools that governments use to make decisions about people.

fraud-detection-and-finance.context_blurb: Long before chatbots, banks and card networks were among the first big businesses to put machine learning to everyday use. Every time a card is swiped or a payment is sent, software decides in a fraction of a second whether to let it through, and occasionally it blocks a purchase and sends the cardholder a text. Most people only notice these systems on the rare day they step in. Finance uses automation elsewhere too: trading firms run programs that buy and sell faster than any human could follow, and those programs react to each other at machine speed. This topic covers how these behind-the-scenes systems make their calls, what they get right, and what can happen when fast automated systems meet each other with no human in between. It matters because these decisions touch nearly everyone who has a bank card or a savings account.

ai-and-jobs.context_blurb: Every wave of AI arrives with predictions about which jobs it will wipe out. By the mid-2020s there was real evidence to look at. Companies in customer service, stock photography, and other fields had put generative AI to work, some of them announcing large cuts to human staff, and independent studies and sales figures began to show what had actually changed. The picture that emerged was more mixed than either the boosters or the doomsayers had predicted. This topic looks at specific industries where AI was rolled out at scale: which parts of the work it took over, which parts it did not, and how customers reacted. A job is a bundle of many different tasks, so the useful question to ask of any 'AI will replace this profession' headline is which tasks inside the job are meant.
